Thermodynamic and economic comparison of pressure shift freezing and isochoric pressurization without a hyperbaric pump

# Boris Rubinsky · Alan Maida · Cristina Bilbao-Sainz

Received: 2 April 2026 / Accepted: 11 September 2026 This is a U.S. Government work and not under copyright protection in the US; foreign copyright protection may apply 2026

Abstract Pressure-assisted freezing produces frozen foods with finer ice crystals, less drip loss and longer microbiologi­ cal shelf life than conventional freezing, but its adoption has been limited because the conventional implemen­ tation, pressure-shift freezing (PSF), requires a hyperbaric pump delivering 100–200 MPa whose capital cost and mechanical complexity are the principal barrier to industrial deployment. A rigid constant-volume chamber cooled in a standard industrial freezer reaches the same pressurized subzero state passively, because partial ice formation in a confined volume drives the pressure along the ice Ih liquidus; this eliminates the pump at the cost of freezing sacrificial water, an overhead that grows with subzero depth. This work compares the two routes thermodynamically on an equal-output basis, from the ambient inlet state to the common pressurized subzero state that both must reach, with all water and ice properties evaluated from the IAPWS formulations. The two paths differ in a way that is thermodynamically fundamental: the PSF vessel is a moving-boundary system held at constant pressure by its pump, so its cooling duty is an enthalpy change and the pump must also supply boundary work as the fluid contracts, whereas the isochoric chamber is rigid, so its duty is an internalenergy change and no external work is supplied at all. Per kilogram of product delivered to the common state, isochoric pressurization consumes 53–87 kJ kg⁻¹ less electrical energy than batch PSF between − 5 and − 20 °C, and is competitive with an aspirational continuous flow-through PSF architecture above approximately − 9.4 °C. The crossover between the two routes is governed by the ratio of pumping to refrigeration efficiency rather than by either efficiency individually. Because the analysis stops at the shared state, the comparison is indepen­ dent of what is done downstream, and applies equally to isochoric preservation, in which the product is held unfrozen at that state, and to the hypothetical use of the isochoric chamber as a pressure generator for a subse­ quent decompression-nucleation step. The framework identifies batch operation, rather than the choice between mechanical and isochoric pressurization, as the dominant thermodynamic liability of conventional PSF.

## Introduction

Pressure-assisted freezing exploits the negative slope of the ice Ih–liquid coexistence curve: increasing pressure depresses the equilibrium freezing temperature of water, opening a thermodynamic window in which biologi­ cal materials can be held simultaneously at elevated pressure and subzero temperature1–3. When the pressure is subsequently released, the contents of the vessel are projected far below the atmospheric-pressure liquidus and rapidly nucleate ice throughout their bulk. The resulting ice microstructure is finer and more uniformly dis­ tributed than that produced by conventional surface-driven freezing. The benefit has been demonstrated across distinct product classes: in model gel systems, where matrix structure and rehydration behavior are improved4; in vegetable tissue, where potato cubes show improved texture, color and microstructure5; in fish and seafood, where salmon develops finer ice crystals than in classical freezing6 and smoked salmon mince shows microbial inactivation7; and in meat and marine products more generally8. The phenomenon and its thermodynamic basis are reviewed by LeBail and co-workers9 and by Li and Sun10, and the associated terminology is defined by Urru­ tia Benet and colleagues11.

An implementation of high pressure processing is pressure-shift freezing (PSF)12. In PSF a product is loaded into a rigid pressure vessel together with a transmitting fluid (typically water or a glycol mixture), pressurized by a hydraulic intensifier or plunger pump to 100–200 MPa, cooled to a subzero temperature while the contents remain liquid, and then rapidly decompressed. The amount of ice formed instantaneously on decompression has been quantified by Otero and Sanz13, and the resulting microstructure compared against high-pressure-assisted freezing by Fernández and co-workers14. The thermodynamic path is 1 → 2′ → 2 → 3 in Fig. 1A: ambient (1) → pressurization at room temperature (2′) → cooling at constant pressure to the target state (2) → atmospheric supercooling and nucleation (3). Despite the documented product-quality advantages6,15,16, PSF has not achieved widespread industrial deployment in food preservation. Hyperbaric intensifiers, dynamic high-pressure seals, and the autofrettage or composite-overwrap vessels that house them represent a multi-million-dollar capital expenditure and operate as a batch process that further penalises throughput.

Isochoric freezing-driven pressurization (IFP) offers a thermodynamically distinct route to the same pres­ surized liquid–ice equilibrium without an external pressurizing pump. The physical principles are reviewed by Consiglio and co-workers22, the temperature–volume phase behavior is mapped by Powell-Palm23,28, and the multiphase thermodynamic theory has been validated experimentally1,23. A rigid, constant-volume chamber is filled with the product and an aqueous medium and cooled in a standard industrial freezer. Because ice Ih is less dense than liquid water, partial ice formation in a confined volume forces the system pressure to rise along the liquidus curve until thermal equilibrium is reached at the freezer setpoint. The thermodynamic path is 1 → 2” → 2→ 3 in Fig. 1A. Our experiments show that the sealing temperature of the isochoric chamber strongly affects the freezing process. Water expands as it warms above freezing. Therefore, the sealing temperature changes the cooling path inside the chamber. The internal pressure and ice fraction are uniquely determined by the tempera­ ture and by the state at which the chamber was sealed. Therefore, in our experiments we systematically seal the chamber at 0 °C. Starting from 0 °C, the isochoric freezing process follows the liquidus line (Fig. 1B); at − 20 °C the internal pressure reaches 194 MPa with an ice fraction of 0.55. From a capital-cost perspective, IFP replaces the hyperbaric pump, intensifier, dynamic seals and high-cycle pressure vessel of PSF with a static rigid container cooled by ordinary industrial refrigeration. The price of this simplification is a thermodynamic one: a fraction φ of the water in the chamber must be frozen to generate the pressure, so to deliver one kilogram of unfrozen pressurized liquid at state 2 the system must process a total of 1/(1 − φ) ≥ 1 kg of mass. The corresponding massscaling factor r = 1/(1 − φ) rises from 1.34 at − 5 °C to 2.22 at − 20 °C.

Although PSF and isochoric freezing have each been studied extensively, prior work has concentrated on product quality, microbial inactivation, and process phenomenology. Isochoric freezing has been reviewed as an emerging preservation technology24–27, its instrumentation and physicochemical influence surveyed28, and its application demonstrated for chicken breast29,30, orange and carot juice31,32, milk33, a range of horticultural products34–37, microbial and spore inactivation38–41. A rigorous thermodynamic comparison of the two pressur­ ization strategies on an equal-output basis, quantifying the energetic price of the IFP sacrificial freezing against the energetic price of the PSF decompression event at a common end state, has not previously been established. The economic framing of the choice between the two technologies has therefore rested on capital-cost arguments alone, without an underlying physical accounting of the recurring operating-energy cost in either direction.

The present work develops a common thermodynamic framework for comparing the two routes on an equaloutput basis. The contribution is fivefold. First, all thermophysical properties are taken directly from the IAPWS formulations, so that no constant specific heat, constant latent heat or constant specific volume enters the energy or exergy balance. Second, the minimum freezing exergy required to produce one kilogram of useful frozen product is derived explicitly from first principles, providing a reversible benchmark independent of equipment choices. Third, the cycle-level pressurization efficiency of batch PSF is derived bottom-up from the componentlevel plunger-pump efficiency, making the decompression-loss term falsifiable and traceable to a standard hard­ ware specification. Fourth, a three-way comparison of batch PSF, continuous flow-through processing and IFP is conducted over − 5 to − 20 °C. Fifth, a sensitivity analysis establishes the structural result that the crossover between IFP and flow-through PSF depends on the two equipment efficiencies only through their ratio. The central question is operational and economic: when does eliminating the hyperbaric pump in favor of sacrificial isochoric freezing produce a net reduction in operating-energy cost per kilogram of useful frozen product, and when does it not?

## Methods

Scope and assumptions

The analysis is a cycle-level thermodynamic comparison between two pressure-generation strategies at an equiv­ alent processing endpoint. The following assumptions are adopted throughout and applied uniformly to both PSF and IFP.

i. Quasi-equilibrium operation: each process is treated as a sequence of equilibrium states along its ther­ modynamic path. Transient thermal gradients, finite cooling rates, and finite decompression rates are not modeled. This is a modeling choice of the present work rather than an established convention, and its consequences are examined in Sect. 5.5. ii. Negligible nucleation kinetics and crystal-morphology effects on the energy balance: ice nucleation and crystal growth are essential to the product-quality argument for pressure-assisted freezing but do not enter the first-law or second-law balance per kilogram of frozen product. The kinetics of instantaneous ice formation on decompression are treated separately in the literature13. iii. Negligible vessel wall heat capacity, ancillary thermal mass, and product non-aqueous heat capacity: the refrigeration duty is computed for the water content of the system. The asymmetry this introduces between the two routes is quantified in Sect. 5.5. iv. The pressure-transmitting medium in PSF is water, and the pressurizing pump is a positive-displacement plunger/intensifier whose component-level mechanical efficiency is in the range of in line-eq-IEq1 ≈ 0.8542,43. The cycle-level effectiveness of this pump under batch operation is derived in Sect. 2.7 rather than assumed, in the manner of the audit of Atuonwu and Tassou20. v. The refrigeration plant is shared between PSF and IFP: a single industrial cascade refrigeration system delivers cold to either process, and its temperature-dependent coefficient of performance is computed from the Carnot limit with a fixed second-law efficiency factor44,45.

Under these assumptions the comparison is a thermodynamic equivalence in the sense of equal output mass at equal end state, not a claim of identical kinetics, microstructure, or product quality. The product-quality implica­ tions are discussed in Sect.  5.4.

Where the comparison begins and ends

Both routes start at state A, product and water at ambient temperature and atmospheric pressure, and both must reach state 2, the target subzero temperature T at the corresponding liquidus pressure p(T). The paths between these states differ, and the present analysis is confined to that difference. In PSF the charge is pressurized at ambient temperature (step B) and then cooled under pressure to the target temperature (step C). In the isochoric route the charge is cooled to 0 °C at atmospheric pressure (step B) and then cooled further within the sealed rigid chamber, where progressive ice formation raises the pressure along the liquidus until the target state is reached (step C).

Everything downstream of state 2 is common to the two routes and cancels. In pressure-shift freezing the pres­ sure is released, the supercooled liquid nucleates throughout its bulk, the latent heat released returns the product to approximately 0 °C, and the partially frozen product is then cooled to its storage temperature at atmospheric pressure. That sequence is identical whether state 2 was reached mechanically or isochorically, and modeling it would add the same quantity to both sides of the comparison. Restricting the analysis to steps B and C therefore removes a large common term without loss of generality.

It also confines the comparison to processes that have been demonstrated, which requires care to state pre­ cisely. Isochoric preservation as practiced to date does not proceed beyond state 2: the product is held unfro­ zen within the unfrozen fraction at the temperature and pressure of that state, and the chamber is subsequently

Cycle-level pressurization efficiency for batch PSF

The single most consequential modeling choice in comparing PSF to IFP is the pressurization efficiency assigned to the PSF pumping system, because pump electrical energy is exactly the cost that IFP avoids. We distinguish a component-level efficiency in line-eq-IEq35, the steady-state head efficiency of the pressurizing device operating continu­ ously, taken here as 0.85, a value assumed rather than measured and lying within the range typical of reciprocat­ ing positive-displacement pumps; the sensitivity analysis of Sect.  4.4 shows that the comparison depends on this quantity only through its ratio to the refrigeration efficiency, which is why an assumed value is tolerable, from a cycle-level effectiveness, the fraction of electrical energy drawn by the entire pressurizing subsystem that appears as net useful pressure work on the product over a complete batch pressurize–hold–decompress cycle.

For a single-vessel batch installation, three mechanisms reduce the cycle-level effectiveness. (a) Decompres­ sion energy loss: at the end of every cycle the pressurized fluid is vented, and the elastic energy stored in the compressed water, equal in magnitude to Wp, is dissipated irreversibly. (b) Water compressibility: the additional fluid displaced by compression must also be pumped, and that work is likewise lost on decompression. (c) Idle and ancillary loads during the hold phase. ## Discussion

Batch versus continuous operation: the dominant variable

The most striking finding of the three-way comparison is that the difference between batch PSF and flow-through PSF, both of which use mechanical pressurization, is consistently larger than the difference between mechanical and isochoric pressurization at fixed operating mode. At − 15 °C the batch-versus-flow-through energy difference is 125 kJ kg⁻¹, while the flow-through-versus-isochoric difference is 41 kJ kg⁻¹. The dominant thermodynamic liability of PSF as currently practiced is the irrecoverable decompression event at the end of every batch cycle, not the use of a mechanical pump per se. This has two consequences. First, attention paid to mechanical energy recovery addresses a larger fraction of the PSF inefficiency than improvements in pump head efficiency alone. Second, a comparison of PSF and IFP that uses the steady-state plunger-pump efficiency of 0.85 for PSF, as is sometimes done, is thermodynamically inconsistent for a batch process and substantially understates the energy cost of PSF as actually operated. Equations (11) and (12) provide an explicit, falsifiable correction.

Combining the operating-energy comparison with the capital-cost argument, three regimes emerge. (i) At tar­ get temperatures above approximately − 10 °C, IFP is energetically equivalent to, or modestly preferable to, even an idealized flow-through PSF system that does not currently exist commercially; because IFP addition­ ally eliminates the hyperbaric-pump capital expenditure, it dominates PSF on every axis in this regime. (ii) Between approximately − 10 and − 15 °C, IFP remains competitive with idealized flow-through PSF and retains an 84–87 kJ kg⁻¹ energy advantage over the real industrial alternative, batch PSF, while its exergy advantage passes through zero near − 11.7 °C. (iii) Below approximately − 15 °C, the sacrificial-freezing penalty grows large enough that an idealized flow-through system would be preferred if available; in its absence IFP remains prefer­ able to batch PSF on energy grounds but loses on exergy grounds.

Which route is preferred for a given application therefore turns on a single quantity: the target temperature at state 2 that the application requires. That target is set by the intended downstream use, and it should not be confused with the storage temperature of the finished product, which is reached later by conventional means and lies outside the present comparison. Wherever the required state-2 temperature is milder than the crossover, the isochoric route is preferred against every PSF architecture considered here; for colder targets it remains preferred against the batch equipment that is actually available, though an idealized continuous system would be better still. Because the crossover lies at − 9.4 °C under the most conservative assumption and moves below − 20 °C at the filling efficiencies specified for commercial vessels, the isochoric route is preferred across most of the range examined. A processor evaluating the two technologies should locate the crossover for their own plant from the efficiency ratio of Eq. (14) rather than adopt the generic value quoted here.

Beyond state 2: product quality

Because the comparison terminates at state 2, product quality lies outside it. Two observations are nonetheless worth recording. First, the two routes deliver different chamber contents at that state: a PSF vessel holds the product in liquid transmitting fluid, whereas an isochoric chamber holds it among inl i ne -eq-IEq93= 25–55% ice. Whether that ice acts as a thermal reservoir favorable to subsequent nucleation, or as a mechanical constraint on delicate structures, is an empirical question this framework cannot resolve; it is sharpest at deep temperatures, where the ice fraction is largest, and mildest in the superchilling window where the isochoric route is most favored. Dual-compartment designs that isolate the product within the liquid fraction are the natural response and merit dedicated study. Practical deviations from the idealized assumptions

The assumptions of Sect.  2.1 are applied uniformly to both routes, but uniform application does not by itself guarantee that the comparison is unaffected: what matters is whether the deviation from each assumption in a real installation is symmetric between PSF and IFP. We consider each in turn and identify those that are not.

Product composition

Real foods are 70–90% water, with lower specific heat and lower latent heat per kilogram than pure water, so the refrigeration duty of both routes falls by a similar factor. Because inline-eq-IEq94 is a property of the pressure-generating water in the chamber rather than of the product, the mass-scaling factor is unchanged. The deviation is therefore close to neutral: absolute energies fall for both routes, differences scale approximately in proportion, and the crossover moves little. Solutes do depress the freezing point and modify the liquidus, which is the effect covered by the ± 10% ice-fraction sensitivity of Sect.  4.4.

Vessel thermal mass

This deviation is not symmetric, and it acts against IFP. Both routes require a vessel rated for 100–200 MPa, but the IFP chamber must contain inline-eq-IEq95kilograms of water per kilogram of useful product and is correspondingly larger, so its wall mass per kilogram of product is greater by roughly the same factor. Since the chamber is cooled and rewarmed on each cycle, its heat capacity enters the refrigeration duty directly. For a steel chamber of practical wall thickness the parasitic duty is of the order of several per cent of the water duty per cycle, so the IFP penalty relative to PSF is a few per cent of inline-eq-IEq96 — small compared with the 53–87 kJ kg⁻¹ advantage, but a genuine erosion of it that grows with r and therefore with subzero depth.

Quasi-equilibrium operation and cycle time

This deviation is also asymmetric against IFP. Cooling inline-eq-IEq97kilograms through a conduction-limited path takes lon­ ger than cooling one, so the IFP cycle is longer at fixed refrigeration capacity and accumulates more heat leak per kilogram of product. The energy effect is modest for a well-insulated chamber; the throughput effect is not, and is treated in Sect.  5.6. Transient gradients also mean that a real chamber is never exactly at the uniform state assumed in Eq. (2); the local ice fraction varies through the chamber, and the reported r should be read as a chamber average.

Idealized pressurization

The deviations here act against PSF. Real high-pressure systems lose fluid through dynamic seals, and leakage must be made up by additional pumping work that is entirely lost. Intensifiers operate off their design point during much of the pressurization ramp, so the effective head efficiency is below nameplate. Both effects reduce the true cycle effectiveness below the 0.46 of Eq. (11), which is why the measured audit range extends down to 0.4420. IFP has no analogue of either loss, having no dynamic seal and no pump. The idealization is therefore conservative with respect to the present conclusion rather than favorable to it.

Shared refrigeration plant

The assumption that a single plant serves either process is reasonable at equal target temperature, but a real IFP installation places a larger and more sustained load on the plant, since it must remove r times the latent heat over

Non-energy implementation considerations

Operating energy and equipment capital cost are the two terms the present framework quantifies, but they are not the only terms that determine adoption. Several considerations fall outside the thermodynamic analysis, and they do not all favor the same route.

Maintenance

The dominant consumable-maintenance item in high-pressure food processing is the dynamic high-pressure seal, subject to wear and periodic replacement at intervals set by cycle count, together with the intensifier packing and the associated hydraulic circuit. IFP has no dynamic high-pressure seal and no pump: the chamber closure is a static seal opened and closed at atmospheric pressure and never exposed to sliding contact under load. This removes an entire maintenance category rather than reducing it, and is a substantial part of the practical case for IFP, distinct from the avoided capital cost of the pump itself.

Operational complexity and safety

A PSF installation requires an intensifier skid, hydraulic utilities, high-pressure tubing runs, and the operator training and periodic inspection that pressure equipment attracts under ASME Section VIII or the European Pressure Equipment Directive. An IFP chamber is also a pressure component and remains subject to design and inspection requirements, but it is a sealed vessel with no external pressure circuit, no pressurized lines outside the chamber, and no active pressurization to control; the pressure is a consequence of temperature and is bounded by it, which simplifies both the control system and the failure analysis.

Throughput and cycle time

This consideration works against IFP and is not captured by the per-kilogram energy balance. Because the cham­ ber must cool inline-eq-IEq98kilograms of water per kilogram of useful product, and cooling is conduction-limited, the cycle time at fixed refrigeration capacity scales approximately with inline-eq-IEq99, from about 1.3 times the equivalent PSF freezing time at − 5 °C to about 2.2 times at − 20 °C. Where a line is throughput-limited rather than energy-limited this penalty may dominate the operating-energy advantage entirely, and it must be evaluated per installation. It can be mitigated by chamber geometry that shortens the conduction path, at the cost of a lower ratio of product to chamber wall.

Scalability

The cost of a high-pressure vessel rises steeply with both volume and design pressure, so PSF scales by enlarg­ ing a single expensive vessel and its intensifier. IFP scales by replicating chambers in parallel within a freezer, so capacity is added in small increments with a nearly linear cost and no single point of failure. The counterpart

IFP chambers are cooled by ordinary industrial refrigeration and can in principle be loaded into existing blast freezers, plate freezers or cold rooms, offering an incremental retrofit path within existing plant and existing cold-chain logistics. For a processor evaluating pressure-assisted freezing for the first time, the availability of a lowcommitment pilot within existing infrastructure is a considerable practical advantage of IFP that is independent of the thermodynamic comparison.

Taken together, these considerations reinforce the energy-based case for IFP in the mild-freezing window and partially offset its energy disadvantage at deep temperatures, with the important exception of throughput, which works against IFP at every temperature and increasingly so with subzero depth.

## Conclusions

A common thermodynamic framework was developed to compare two routes to pressure-assisted freezing of foods on an equal-output basis: conventional pressure-shift freezing, which uses a hydraulic pump to deliver 100–200 MPa to a batch processing vessel, and isochoric freezing-driven pressurization, which generates the same pressure passively by partial isochoric freezing of additional water in a rigid container cooled by standard industrial refrigeration. All thermophysical properties were evaluated from the IAPWS formulations, so that the comparison rests on reference equations of state rather than on constant-property approximations. The framework quantifies the recurring operating-energy cost of substituting sacrificial freezing for a hyperbaric pump, the cen­ tral economic trade-off that has so far been argued in capital-cost terms alone.

Under a cycle-level pressurization efficiency derived from the component-level plunger-pump efficiency and accounting for the irrecoverable decompression event at the end of every PSF batch cycle, the isochoric route consumes 53–87 kJ kg⁻¹ less electrical energy than batch PSF across the − 5 to − 20 °C range at the conserva­ tive filling efficiency FE = 1, and far more at realistic filling efficiencies. Against an idealized flow-through PSF system that does not currently exist commercially, IFP is energetically equivalent above approximately − 10 °C and inferior by 3–103 kJ kg⁻¹ at lower temperatures, the latter penalty arising from the mass-scaling factor r = 1/ (1 − φ) intrinsic to isochoric pressurization. The exergy destruction follows the same qualitative pattern with a crossover near − 11.7 °C.

The sensitivity analysis shows that the crossover between IFP and flow-through PSF is governed by the ratio of pumping to refrigeration efficiency rather than by either efficiency individually, and lies between approxi­ mately − 4 °C and − 15 °C over the full plausible parameter range with a baseline near − 10 °C. The energy advantage of IFP over batch PSF is preserved throughout the − 5 to − 15 °C window across every parameter com­ bination tested, and is preserved across the entire tested envelope, and widens substantially once the pressuretransmitting mass of the PSF vessel is accounted for.

The three-way comparison identifies batch operation, rather than the choice between mechanical and isochoric pressurization, as the dominant thermodynamic liability of conventional PSF. Equivalently, the operating-energy cost of eliminating the hyperbaric pump in favor of sacrificial isochoric freezing is small or favorable across the temperature range of practical interest for frozen-food processing. The framework provides a basis for technol­ ogy selection that complements the capital-cost argument by quantifying the recurring operating-energy term, and it locates that basis precisely: the crossover near − 9.4 °C lies above the − 18 °C retail frozen-storage stan­ dard, so IFP is unambiguously preferred in the superchilling and mild-freezing window while, in the deep-freeze

Five challenges remain before either route can be committed to industrial adoption. First, no instrumented energy audit of a complete installation of either route at food-processing scale has been reported, so the cyclelevel effectiveness of Eqs. (11) and (12) and the sensitivity envelopes of Sect.  4.4 remain modeled rather than measured; such audits are the highest-priority validation step. Second, published isochoric work is conducted at laboratory chamber volumes, and demonstration at food-processing scale is required before the throughput and thermal-mass penalties of Sect.  5.5 and 5.6 can be quantified rather than estimated. Third, the effect on prod­ uct quality of the 25–55% ice fraction present in an IFP chamber before decompression is unresolved and must be characterized experimentally for each product class against the well-documented PSF benchmarks. Fourth, chamber geometry and fill protocol have not been optimized; reducing the effective mass-scaling factor below its thermodynamic bound through displacement fixtures, dual-compartment designs, or pre-chilled sealing would directly reduce the principal energy penalty of IFP. Fifth, pressure-assisted freezing as a novel process requires validation against food-safety regulatory frameworks, which for processes of this kind is frequently the ratelimiting step regardless of the thermodynamic case. The framework developed here is intended to inform where that effort is best directed, not to substitute for it.

## Abstract

This study investigated the effects of isochoric freezing (IF) on the shelf-life and quality of raw bovine milk over a 5-week period. The results were compared with conventional refrigeration (RF) and refrigeration after pasteurization (HTST). The IF treatment process entailed storing liquid raw milk in isochoric chambers in thermodynamic equilibrium at −5 °C/77 MPa and −10 °C/96 MPa. Several parameters were analyzed, including microbiology count, physicochemical properties, indigenous enzyme activity, protein content, volatile organic compounds profile, and lipid degradation. Both raw and pasteurized milk experienced increases in the microbial level past the acceptable threshold (≥5.5 log CFU/mL) after 2 weeks and 5 weeks, respectively, leading to the deterioration of other parameters during storage. In comparison, microbiology count decreased significantly during storage for both IF treatment conditions but was more pronounced for the higher pressure (96 MPa) treatment, leading to undetectable levels of microorganism after 5 weeks. IF treatment maintained stable pH, titratable acidity, viscosity, lipid oxidation, volatile profiles, total protein content, and lactoperoxidase activity throughout the storage period. Color was preserved during IF treatment at −5 °C/77 MPa; however, color was impacted during IF treatment at −10 °C/96 MPa. Protein structures were also modified during pressurized storage in both IF treatments. Overall, the study demonstrated that isochoric freezing could significantly increase the shelf-life of milk by reducing microbiology activity, whilst maintaining its nutritional content. These results underscore the potential role of isochoric freezing as a valuable tool in eliminating pathogens while maintaining quality characteristics similar to raw milk over long storage periods.

## 1. Introduction

In light of a growing global population and the challenges posed by climate change and increasingly extreme weather patterns, ensuring food security has become a concern for the global community. Milk, renowned as one of nature’s most complete foods in terms of nutritional value [1], plays a pivotal role in addressing these insecurities. Concurrently, the alarming issue of food waste is taking a hefty toll on it. Across the globe, dairy farmers annually discard milk due to fluctuations in production, experiencing oversupply during peak seasons and shortages in off-peak periods. Other factors contributing to milk disposal include spoilage due to improper practices, a predicament experienced even in some of the most advanced dairy economies, where inappropriate handling leads to 29 million tons of dairy products being wasted due to fungal contamination and microbial attack annually [2]. The cumulative effects of these issues have led to a staggering global estimate of approximately 128 million tons of milk being discarded each year [3]. While current milk production meets consumer demand in many regions, the future presents uncertainties, driven by climate change and an increase in extreme weather patterns. Milk production is highly sensitive to heat stress, where intense summer heat has been shown to reduce milk production by up to 40% [4]. Considering the vital importance of milk and its by-products, such as baby formula, it is increasingly evident that improvements in preservation methods that may aid in waste reduction are needed for food security.

Milk, with its rich nutritional content and physicochemical properties, is an ideal breeding ground for bacteria, making milk one of the riskiest foods in terms of food safety [5]. Current preservation methods, primarily thermal treatment and freezing, offer partial solutions. High-temperature short-time (HTST) pasteurization, for instance, successfully eliminates harmful microorganisms but only extends milk’s shelf life up to 14 days [6]. Another emerging method is ultra-high temperature (UHT) treatment, which is gaining popularity for its ability to sterilize milk by heating it to 140 °C for a couple of seconds [7]. Although this process extends the shelf life of milk to over 30 days, it comes at the cost of significant protein and amino acid modifications that can affect digestibility [8]. Freezing, while prolonging milk’s shelf life for months, significantly decreases the milk’s fat, protein, and lactose contents [9]. Consequently, alternative methods are required to preserve milk.

Non-thermal processing technologies utilizing pressure have emerged as promising alternatives capable of reducing microbial load and thereby extending the shelf-life of milk. One such technique is high-pressure processing (HPP), which subjects milk to pressures ranging from 400 to 600 MPa for just a few seconds. HPP-treated milk, akin to conventionally pasteurized milk, requires refrigeration, but it exhibits the potential to prolong shelf-life for a substantial period, typically between 30 and 45 days [10]. Another innovative method, hyperbaric storage (HS), employs milder pressures, usually in the range of 20 to 150 MPa, for extended treatment durations. In a study by Duarte et al. [11], raw milk was treated at 75–100 MPa and room temperature for 60 days, resulting in microbial inactivation of endogenous microbial load, surrogate, and pathogenic microorganisms, as well as bacterial spores. Remarkably, this approach also preserved the activity of heat-sensitive enzymes that exhibit antimicrobial activity [12]. However, under long-term hyperbaric storage, certain parameters influenced by temperature, such as volatiles and lipid oxidation, exhibited alterations [13]. These findings underscore the potential of mild pressures (75–100 MPa) in both controlling microbial growth and preserving the biochemical activity of milk, and highlight the potential value of the simultaneous optimization of storage temperature.

Isochoric freezing (IF) leverages confined aqueous thermodynamics to passively generate elevated pressures at mild sub-freezing temperatures, producing a technologically simple means of reducing metabolic processes while avoiding formation of ice in the stored food product [14,15]. The process involves filling a rigid container with an aqueous solution and a food product, subjecting it to sub-freezing temperatures, and allowing the expansion of ice to passively pressurize the interior of the system. Per Le Chatelier’s principle, the rising pressure hinders further freezing, inducing a pressurized two-phase liquid–ice equilibrium with a stable ice fraction at any given sub-freezing temperature. The system continues to freeze and increase pressure as the temperature of the system decreases, until it reaches the triple point of ice 1 h, ice III, and the liquid. For pure water, this point occurs at approximately −21 °C and 210 MPa, with approximately 55% of the volume being converted to ice. This controlled freezing process allows food products to be placed within the liquid region of the chamber, preventing ice crystal formation and the according biophysical injury. Previous research has demonstrated the effectiveness of IF in reducing microbial activity and preserving physicochemical properties in various food products, without compromising nutritional content [16,17,18,19,20].

This study aims to contribute to the growing body of knowledge on the potential of isochoric freezing to preserve biological materials. Herein, we investigated the physicochemical and microbiological changes resulting from isochoric freezing of raw milk at temperatures of −5 °C and −10 °C, and respective pressures of 77 and 96 MPa, for storage up to 5 weeks. We assessed key parameters, including pH, titratable acidity, color, viscosity, lactoperoxidase activity, free fatty acids, lipid oxidation, protein content, protein interactions, volatiles, and microbiology counts and compared them to raw milk and conventionally treated HTST milk. Our future research will delve into the effects of prolonged high-pressure exposure on milk shelf-life during subsequent refrigerated storage.

This work presents an initial exploration of the potential of isochoric milk preservation, offering a potentially promising solution to enhance food security, reduce food waste, and provide consumers with safe, nutritious milk after longer storage durations.

## 2. Materials and Methods

### 2.1. Isochoric System

Two different treatment conditions were used for isochoric experiments. Raw milk was treated at −5 °C/77 MPa and −10 °C/96 MPa using a pressure chamber made of Aluminum-7075 with a type-II anodize coating and a total volume capacity of 1500 mL, and pressure-rated for up to 275 MPa (BioChoric Inc., Bozeman, MT, USA). Each chamber was connected to a pressure gauge to monitor the pressure over time. The chambers were cooled using a chest freezer (Magic Chef Model #HMCF9W3, MC Appliance Corporation, Wood Dale, IL, USA).

### 2.2. Experimental Protocol

Raw bovine milk was purchased from a local market located in Albany, California. Four different conditions were compared: refrigerated raw milk (RF), refrigerated milk initially treated with high-temperature short-time (HTST) pasteurization, raw milk held under isochoric freezing (IF) at −5 °C/77 MPa, and raw milk held under IF at −10 °C/96 MPa. These conditions were chosen based on preliminary results in which IF −15 °C/150 MPa led to phase separation in the milk within just one day of storage, rendering them unsuitable for long-term storage.

Initial tests and treatments began seven days before the labeled expiration date of the milk. Refrigerated (RF) raw bovine milk was used as the control. For the HTST treatment, raw bovine milk was heated to 72 °C and pasteurized for 15 s using a multipurpose sterilization unit (UHT/HTST Lab Microthermics model 25EHVH, Raleigh, NC, USA). The pasteurized milk was collected and divided aseptically into 3 sterilized polypropylene bottles through the drain-out line. The initial quality of both RF and HTST milk was immediately tested to measure microbiological activity, physiochemical properties, and retention of certain compounds. The samples were then stored in a refrigerator (4 °C) for up to 5 weeks.

For the IF treatments, samples of the milk were prepared on the same day as the RF and HTST samples. Three bags of about 150 mL of raw bovine milk each were processed for each treatment. The sterilized bags were heat sealed with negligible air bubbles within them and transferred to four separate isochoric chambers (total of twelve bags) filled with cold water. Cold water helped prevent accelerated bacteria growth as the chambers cooled to their preset temperatures in the chest freezers. After the treatment, the chamber was placed in a freezer set at 5 °C for 14 h to melt all the ice within the chamber. Milk samples were treated under isochoric conditions for 2 and 5 weeks.

### 2.3. Microbiology

Decimal dilutions were prepared for total plate count and Pseudomonas. Appropriate dilutions were plated on plate count agar (PCA) for total aerobic mesophiles (TAM) and incubated at 30 °C for 3 days [21].

Numbers of Pseudomonas spp. were determined by spread plating-appropriate dilutions on a Pseudomonas agar base with Cephalothin, Fucidin, and Cetrimide (CFC) supplement (Oxoid Ltd., Basingstoke, Hampshire, UK) and incubated at 25 °C for 72 h.

### 2.4. pH/Titration

The pH of the milk was determined in triplicate using a pH meter (Hanna instruments, Smithfield, RI, USA).

The titratable acidity (TA) of the milk samples was determined by titrating 10 mL of diluted milk (4 mL of milk in 6 mL of DI water) to pH of 8.4 with 0.01 M sodium hydroxide solution. The results were expressed as grams of lactic acid per liter of milk based on: (1) T A = N N a O H × m L N a O H × 90.08 m L o f s a m p l e

### 2.5. Color

The color of the bovine milk was measured using a tristimulus colorimeter (CM508D, Konica-Minolta Inc., Ramsey, NJ, USA) with a sample holder (CM-A128) and an 8 mm diameter target mask (CM-A195). The milk sample (10 mL) was pipetted into the sample holder covered with the black background and the color of each sample was measured three times. Results were expressed as L* (lightness), a* (redness/greenness), and b* (yellowness/blueness) in the CIE Lab system. These values were used to calculate the overall color difference (ΔE*) according to the following equations:(2) ∆ L * = L * − L o * (3) ∆ a = a * − a o * (4) ∆ b = b * − b o * (5) ∆ E * = ∆ L * 2 + ∆ a * 2 + ∆ b * 2 where Lo*, ao*, and bo* represent the initial values prior to storage/treatment at day 0.

### 2.6. Turbidity

Turbidity of milk samples was monitored using a Hach Model TL2300 turbidimeter (Hach Company, Loveland, CO, USA). The instrument was calibrated using StablCal® calibration standards (Hach Company), ranging between <0.1 and 4000 nephelometric turbidity units (NTU). Diluted samples (1 mL of milk in 29 mL of water) were analyzed in a clean sample cell.

### 2.7. Viscosity

Milk viscosity measurements were performed on a DHR-3 rheometer (TA Instrument, New Castle, DE, USA) at 20 °C. A concentric cylinder geometry (28.04 mm bob diameter and 21.10 mm bob length) was used for testing. Three replicates were performed for each sample. For each replicate, 8 mL of milk was pipetted into the concentric cylinder cup and equilibrated at 20 °C for three minutes. The shear rate was increased logarithmically from 0.1 to 200 s−1. The viscosity of the sample was determined at a shear rate of 100 s−1.

### 2.8. Lipid Oxidation

Lipid oxidation was evaluated by quantification of secondary lipid oxidation products with the thiobarbituric acid reactive substances (TBARS) method, which was adapted from the method of Vyncke (1970) [22]. Briefly, 1 mL of milk was mixed with 1 mL of 7.5% trichloroacetic acid in water (TCA) in a 10 mL Falcon tube to allow the release of malondialdehyde (MDA) from the matrix and to precipitate some proteins. This was followed by centrifugation at 6000 rpm for 15 min at 4 °C. Subsequently, 1 mL of the supernatant was added to 1 mL of 2-thiobarbituric acid (20 mM TBA in 99% acetic acid glacial), slightly shaken and heated in a boiling water bath (100 °C for 40 min), and immediately cooled on ice for 5 min. The absorbance of the resulting pink reaction product was measured at 538 nm and room temperature (20 °C) (Microplate Spectrophotometer Multiskan GO, Thermo Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) against a blank-containing TCA instead of the sample. Measurements were performed in triplicate. For quantification, a standard curve of MDA was obtained from the hydrolysis of 1,1,3,3-tetramethoxypropane (Sigma Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA), ranging from 0.5 to 10.0 µM MDA. The results were expressed as µg MDA/mL of milk.

### 2.9. Protein Content

The total protein content was quantified according to the Lowry Method. The samples were diluted twice, (1:9 v/v) and (1:8 v/v), with 0.9% saline solution. The method was performed according to Waterborg and Matthews [23]. A calibration curve (R2 = 0.97) using a protein standard from 50 to 2000 μg/mL was used to quantify the protein content.

### 2.10. Sodium Dodecyl Sulfate-Polyacrylamide Gel Electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE)

The SDS-PAGE analyses were conducted with or without a reducing agent. For nonreduced sample preparation, 5 μL of milk was diluted with 50 μL of Tris-Glycine Native Sample Buffer (Novex, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) and 45 μL of milli-Q water in a 2 mL plastic tube. For reduced samples, 5 μL of milk was diluted with 50 μL of Tris-Glycine SDS Sample Buffer (Novex, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and 35 μL of milli-Q water. Ten μL of sample reducing agent (NuPAGE, Thermo Fisher Scientific) was added to the mixture. Prepared reduced samples were shaken for 10 s and incubated at 85 °C for 2 min. Samples were analyzed using 10 to 20% precast tris-glycine protein mini gels (Invitrogen, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and Mini-Protein Electrophoresis Cells (Invitrogen, Thermo Fisher Scientific). Prestained Protein Ladder (NuPAGE, Thermo Fisher Scientific) was used to identify the detected proteins. Twenty microliters of each sample were added into the injection port and ran at 120 V for 90 min. The gels were stained with SimplyBlueTM (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and then destained with milli-Q water.

### 2.11. Lactoperoxidase Activity

The lactoperoxidase (LPO) activity assay was performed based on the method described by Marín et al. [24]. Briefly, milk was mixed with a solution of 0.65 mM ABTS (in 0.1 M sodium phosphate buffer, pH 6.0) and left for 30 min at 20 °C. Then, 0.1 mM hydrogen peroxide was added and mixed quickly to initiate the reaction, with the absorbance (Abs412nm) measured for 1 min. The enzymatic activity was calculated as the slope of Abs increment as a function of time and expressed as ΔAbs412nm AU/min. All enzymatic assays were performed in triplicate for each storage condition.

The residual activity was calculated by using: (6) R e s i d u a l a c t i v i t y % = ( A A 0 ) ∗ 100 % where A is the enzymatic activity in milk samples after storage and A0 represents the initial enzymatic activity prior to storage.

### 2.12. Volatile Organic Compounds

Volatile organic compounds (VOCs) in the milk samples were measured using headspace solid-phase microextraction (HS-SPME) techniques. Sample preparation methods closely followed procedures described by Lemos et al. [13] with few modifications. Briefly, 10 mL of milk, 3.7 g of sodium chloride, 250 µL of internal standard (aqueous cyclohexanone solution at 25 µg/mL), and a magnetic stir bar were added to a 240 mL screw top amber vial and sealed with a PTFE/silicone septum (22 mm × 2.54 mm thickness) and plastic screw cap combination. Sample vials were subsequently equilibrated in a water bath at 50 °C and gently stirred using a magnetic stir plate (80 rpm). Prior to extraction, the SPME fiber (DVB/CAR/PDMS, 50/30 µm coating, 2 cm length) was heated in the injection port (250 °C) of an Agilent 7890B gas chromatograph for 15 min.

After temperature equilibration of the sample vial, the SPME fiber was exposed to the headspace for 30 min while stirring. Fibers were then desorbed for 10 min (splitless) on a gas chromatograph (7890B) coupled to a mass selective detector (5977A MSD; Agilent Technologies, Palo Alto, CA, USA). The injector temperature was set at 250 °C. A 60 m × 0.25 mm df = 0.25 µm DB-1 fused silica capillary column was used, using helium as a carrier gas at a constant flow of 1 mL/min (99.999% purity). The GC oven was programmed with the following conditions: 35 °C (5 min), ramped at 4 °C/min until 100 °C, a second ramp at 10 °C/min until 220 °C, and finally held at 220 °C (5 min). The purge valve to split vent was opened after 1 min at a flowrate of 30 mL/min following sample injection. The total run time lasted approximately 45 min. The MS transfer line and ion source were maintained at 250 °C and 230 °C, respectively. The MS quadrupole temperature was set to 150 °C with an electron ionization of 70 eV, which was set to full scan mode (m/z 20 to 350 at 1.6 scan/s).

MassHunter Unknowns Analysis software (v. B.07.01) was used for data processing using the deconvolution algorithm. Identification of the VOCs was based on a combination of computer matching with mass spectral libraries (NIST 14) and retention index values derived from an n-alkane solution (c5 to n-c18) (Sigma Aldrich Co.). Only compounds with match factor scores ≥ 70 and signal-to-noise ratios ≥ 10 were selected for quantitation. Semi-quantitation was performed using cyclohexanone as the internal standard (IS). Results are expressed in µg eq. IS per 100 mL of milk.

### 2.13. Statistical Analysis

All experiments and analyses were carried out in triplicate. Analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed under all the different storage conditions, followed by a multiple comparison post hoc test, Tukey’s HSD test, at a 5% level of significance. Additionally, principal component analysis (PCA) was performed in order to identify the statistical patterns in VOC data.

## 3. Results and Discussion

### 3.1. Microbiological Evaluation

Given that raw milk is not inherently sterile, our initial steps included conducting microbiological assessments to evaluate the impact of different treatments and storage conditions on indigenous microorganisms. Psychotropic bacteria are known to be key indicators of milk spoilage. These critical spoilage species include gram-negative bacteria, such as Pseudomonas fluorescens and Pseudomonas fragi [25,26,27,28]. As key indicators of milk quality, these spoilage species can be effectively assessed through total bacteria count (TPC) and Pseudomonas spp. (PS) microbiological quality indexes. Table 1 shows microbial populations found in RF, HTST, and IF-treated milk samples. The initial TPC and PS of raw milk were 6.98 ± 0.05 log CFU mL−1 and 7.22 ± 0.13 log CFU mL−1, respectively. After 2 weeks, the RF sample presented higher counts for both TPC and PS, 8.26 ± 0.19 and 8.07 ± 0.09 log CFU mL−1, respectively. Both initial and storage values were consistent with a previous study [25]. The RF samples in this study were well past their microbial shelf-life after 2 weeks (≥5.5 log CFU mL−1), and no further analyses were performed for these samples. Immediately after HTST treatment, the milk sample reached counts below 1 log CFU mL−1 (detection limit) for both TPC and PS, demonstrating HTST’s effectiveness in deactivating microorganisms. Interestingly, after 2 weeks of refrigerated storage at 4 °C, both TPC and PS for the HTST sample had increased by more than 5 log CFU mL−1. As expected, the HTST sample stored for 5 weeks at 4 °C contained higher microbial load levels, well above the acceptable threshold (≥5.5 log CFU mL−1). A previous study reported similar results for refrigerated HTST treated milk [6].

Isochoric freezing affects microbial viability by potentially disrupting non-covalent bonds and cell membranes at high pressures. Prolonged exposure to these pressures can ultimately result in cell destruction and microbial deactivation [26]. After 2 weeks, the IF (−5 °C) treatment reduced the TPC and PS counts to 3.60 ± 0.12 log CFU mL−1 and to 4.85 ± 0.26 log CFU mL−1, respectively. The IF (−10 °C) treatment resulted in even greater reductions in TPC and PS counts after 2 weeks, 1.26 ± 0.24 and 3.45 ± 0.04 log CFU mL−1, respectively. After prolonged exposure to pressure, microbial counts decreased even further. After 5 weeks, IF (−5 °C) treatment resulted in more than 5 log CFU mL−1 reduction for both TPC and PS counts. For the IF (−10 °C) treatment after 5 weeks, both TPC and PS values were below the detection limit. The positive effect of isochoric freezing on the reducing native microbial populations has been reported in a previous study [18]. A significantly higher reduction was achieved at higher pressures of IF (−10 °C) treatment compared to IF (−5 °C) treatment. Erkmen and Doğan [27] also found that HPP at 400 MPa and 600 MPa for 10 min reduced TPC in raw milk by 2 and 5 log CFU/mL, respectively. Another study showed that HPP treated homogenized milk stored at 4 °C had a microbiological shelf-life similar to that of pasteurized (90 °C for 15 s) milk [28]. This study demonstrated that within just two weeks, IF treatment significantly reduced microbial load levels below those of both RF (refrigeration) and HTST-treated milk. These findings suggest that IF treatment could extend the microbiological shelf-life beyond that of untreated and pasteurized milk.

### 3.2. pH and Titratable Acidity

The pH and titratable acidity of the different milk samples under different storage conditions are shown in Table 2. The initial pH value of raw milk was 6.84 ± 0.04, which was not significantly different from the initial value of 6.82 ± 0.01 following HTST treatment. These values are similar to values reported in the literature [29]. After two weeks of storage, the pH value of the RF sample decreased significantly to 6.57 ± 0.03, while the pH value of the HTST treated milk remained relatively stable at 6.80 ± 0.01. The decrease in the pH value of the milk sample was probably caused by the accumulation of lactic acid produced by lactic acid bacteria. A previous study found that a decrease in pH value only occurred when microbial levels reached >6.5 log CFU mL−1 [29], which was consistent with the microbial numbers reported in Table 1. For IF treated samples, the pH values after 2 weeks at −5 °C and −10 °C showed no significant changes, with pH values of 6.77 ± 0.01 and 6.79 ± 0.02, respectively. Kim et al. [30] obtained comparable results with high pressure (200 MPa) and low temperature (−4 °C) treatments of raw milk for 10, 20, and 30 min. The authors found the treatments had no significant effects on the pH levels of the milk samples. After 5 weeks, the pH value of the HTST treated milk had decreased significantly to 6.63 ± 0.0, which could be explained by the microbial count of >6.5 log CFU mL−1. For IF treatments, the pH values after 5 weeks at −5 °C (6.77 ± 0.01) and −10 °C (6.79 ± 0.02) showed no significant changes compared to the initial values. These results were consistent with the microbial count results, with both samples having microbial levels well below 6.5 log CFU mL−1.

The initial titratable acidity (TA) value for the raw milk was 1.27 ± 0.08 g/L lactic acid, which was similar to the initial value of 1.36 ± 0.08 for HTST treated milk. After 2 weeks, the TA value for the RF sample showed a significant increase to 2.06 ± 0.03 g/L, whereas the TA value for the HTST treated sample remained at 1.35 ± 0.05 g/L. These values were consistent with those found in the literature [11]. In addition, the TA values after 2-week IF treatment at −5 °C (1.35 ± 0.05 g/L) and −10 °C (1.37 ± 0.02) showed no significant changes compared with the initial value. After 5 weeks, the TA values for all milk samples increased significantly (p < 0.05), albeit at different rates. The TA value for the HTST sample reached 1.69 ± 0.02 g/L, whereas the TA values for the IF (−5 °C) and IF (−10 °C) samples reached 1.58 ± 0.06 g/L and 1.63 ± 0.06 g/L, respectively. The increase in TA values might be due to the continual growth of lactic acid bacteria (LAB), leading to more acidic conditions. A previous study reported a positive correlation between acidity and microorganism growth [31]. High-pressure treatment can lead to changes in the buffer capacity of milk, as noted in a study by Salaün [32]. This difference in buffering capacity is likely attributed to changes in casein and the nature of calcium phosphate, both of which are key buffer components, during the pressurization process. These changes in buffering capacity can impact the milk’s response to changes in acidity and may contribute to the observed increase in TA over time.

### 3.3. Color and Turbidity

Appearance is the first relevant attribute that determines whether a product is accepted or rejected by consumers. The appearance of the raw milk samples is shown in Figure 1. Fresh raw milk showed a thick layer of separation between the cream and the serum. After refrigeration for 2 and 5 weeks, the milk showed precipitation that resulted in fewer particles being present in the soluble phase. The HTST milk refrigerated for 5 weeks showed this same appearance. These changes may be related to the spoilage of milk by microorganisms that contributed to protein coagulation and fat degradation. The fresh raw milk and IF (−5 °C) sample showed no perceived differences in visual appearance. In comparison, the IF (−10 °C) sample showed the formation of small and slightly visible aggregates.

Table 3 shows the color parameters (L*, a*, b*) and turbidity values for all samples. Fresh raw milk had an L* value of 77.55 ± 0.15, an a* value of −1.78 ± 0.05, and a b* value of 3.38 ± 0.02. All samples undergoing different treatments and durations showed no significant changes (p < 0.05) in L* values compared to the initial value. The natural color of milk (yellowish white) is ascribed to scattering and absorption of the visible light spectrum by dispersed fat globules, calcium caseinate, calcium phosphate, and pigments [33]. Previous studies found that L* tended to decrease significantly in value after HPP treatment [25]. This could be due to higher applied pressures in HPP treatment (300–600 MPa) compared to IF treatment (75–100 MPa). In addition, none of the treatments resulted in major changes in a* values (greenness). However, the b* (yellowness) value for the HTST sample significantly decreased to 0.03 ± 0.14 after 5 weeks. In comparison, the b* values for the IF (−5 °C) sample were comparable to that of the initial milk sample. Additionally, the b* values for the IF (−10 °C) sample at 2 and 5 weeks significantly increased in value to 4.86 ± 0.01 and 5.14 ± 0.15, respectively. These results were consistent with those reported by Stratakos et al. [25] and Lemos et al. [34] who also observed an increase in the yellowness (increase in b*) of raw milk treated with high pressures. They attributed the behavior to decreases in casein micelles and fat globule sizes due to high pressure that caused light to scatter [35].

The total color change (ΔE) values for the milk samples are shown in Table 3. ΔE is classified as not noticeable (0–0.5), slightly noticeable (0.5–1.5), noticeable (1.5–3.0), well visible (3.0–6.0), and great (6.0–12.0) [36]. According to this classification, the color difference in the HTST sample after 5 weeks is considered to be well visible to the human eye (3.84 ± 0.19). This was mainly caused by the increase in yellowness (b*) due to the increase in microbial loading (≥5.5 log CFU/mL). In comparison, the IF (−5 °C) sample had a slightly noticeable color changes after 2 and 5 weeks, with values of 1.30 ± 0.04 and 1.50 ± 0.2, respectively. On the other hand, the IF (−10 °C) sample had noticeable color changes after 2 and 5 weeks, with values of 1.56 ± 0.01 and 1.88 ± 0.21, respectively. The increase in total color change for the IF (−10 °C) sample at 5 weeks could be due to the formation of small aggregates.

The initial turbidity value for raw milk was 2325 ± 175 NTU (Table 3). HTST treatment reduced milk turbidity due to alterations of the casein micelles [37]. The turbidity of the milk after IF (−5 °C) treatment was significantly reduced to 2107 and 1720 NTU after 2 and 5 weeks, respectively. Previous authors also found a reduction in turbidity with pressure [38]. In contrast, the turbidity of the milk after IF (−10 °C) treatment increased to 2810 and 3365 NTU after 2 and 5 weeks, respectively. Milk turbidity was mainly related to the aggregation and dissociation of casein micelles [39]. The casein micelles are composed of casein molecules, colloidal calcium phosphate, and water molecules dispersed in the whey serum. Depending on the pressure and treatment time, casein micelles can either increase or decrease in size [40]. Disruption of casein micelles into submicelles under pressure could have reduced the turbidity of the IF (−5 °C) milk samples. Anema et al. [39] suggested that the dissociation of casein micelles with pressure could be due to the disruption of hydrophobic and electrostatic interactions, and the solubilization of colloidal calcium phosphate. The increase in turbidity levels in the IF (−10 °C) sample might be due to an increase in casein micelle size from the formation of casein aggregates and complexation of denatured whey protein with casein micelles [40]. These changes in turbidity values were consistent with ΔE results, where the IF (−10 °C) sample had noticeable color change for both treatment time periods.

### 3.4. Viscosity

A comparison of the viscosity values at 100 s−1 between different treatments is shown in Figure 2. The initial viscosity of fresh raw milk was 3.56 ± 0.01 mPa ∗ s. The HTST sample showed a slight decrease in milk viscosity to 3.38 ± 0.01 mPa ∗ s. The decrease in viscosity for heat treated samples has been attributed to a decrease in particle size when milk samples were heated to 60–70 °C [41]. The increase in viscosity values of HTST samples during storage might be due to microbial spoilage. IF (−5 °C) treatment did not cause a clear effect on viscosity values. In comparison, IF (−10 °C) treatment resulted in significant increases in viscosity, with the largest viscosity value of 3.71 ± 0.02 mPa ∗ s after 2 weeks. Previous studies showed increases in viscosity of milk with application of pressure [34,42,43]. The authors of the studies attributed the viscosity increase to the high pressures causing changes in the shape of casein micelles from roughly spherical to irregularly shaped particles due to a significant disruption of micelles and the denaturation of whey proteins [40].

### 3.5. Lipid Oxidation

Lipid oxidation occurs in lipid-rich foods such as milk and is an indicator of oxidative rancidity. The initial TBARS value of raw milk was 0.62 ± 0.02 µg MDA/mL, consistent with values reported in reference [13]. Figure 3 shows the TBARS values of the milk samples. Refrigeration caused about a 50% increase in lipid oxidation after 2 weeks. HTST samples also showed increased lipid oxidation during storage, reaching a value of 1.55 ± 0.19 µg MDA/mL (148% increase) after 5 weeks. This increase in lipid oxidation might be due to microbial and lipase activity. In comparison, IF treatments showed the lowest lipid oxidation values, with no significant differences compared to the fresh sample. After two weeks, the TBARS values for IF (−5 °C) and IF (−10 °C) samples were 0.63 ± 0.16 and 0.86 ± 0.14 µg MDA/mL, respectively. After 5 weeks, these values remained relatively stable for the IF (−5 °C) and IF (−10 °C) samples at 0.69 ± 0.04 and 0.66 ± 0.04 µg MDA/mL, respectively. Previous studies on hyperbaric storage of milk at pressures of 75–100 MPa found higher overall TBARS values at room temperature (20 °C) storage for 60 days compared to refrigerated storage at 4 °C [13].

### 3.6. Protein Content and SDS-PAGE

The total protein content of all samples was determined using the Lowry protein assay. The initial total protein content of raw milk was 32.16 ± 3.33 mg/mL, similar to values reported in reference [44]. The total protein content in HTST treated milk showed an overall significant decrease in value to 23.53 ± 2.33 mg/mL, which was attributed to an increase in proteolytic activity produced by the microflora of milk. In comparison, the protein contents after IF treatments showed no significant changes when compared with the initial values and remained stable throughout the storage period. The total protein contents of the IF (−5 °C) sample were 30.57 ± 0.20 mg/mL after 2 weeks and 30.77 ± 0.42 mg/mL after 5 weeks. Furthermore, the total protein contents of the IF (−10 °C) sample were 30.50 ± 0.66 mg/mL after 2 weeks and 32.17 ± 0.46 mg/mL after 5 weeks (Figure 4). A previous study also found that 60 days of hyperbaric storage at a pressures of 75–100 MPA did not affect the protein contents in milk [12].

Figure 5 shows the SDS-PAGE results for the milk samples under native (A) and reducing (B) conditions. The protein bands for RF milk at week 2 and HTST-treated milk at week 5 appeared with low intensity, indicating a decrease in soluble protein content attributed to an increase in the microbial load levels (Table 1). Surprisingly, under native conditions, all samples showed large molecular weight proteins near the top that could not diffuse into the gel as well as in the absence of whey proteins. The α-casein and β-casein seemed to be unaffected by HTST treatment. Under reducing conditions, all the large molecular weight proteins disappeared, and the κ-casein and whey proteins appeared in the gels. This pattern was also previously observed in heat-treated bovine milk [45]. The large aggregates that could not diffuse into the gels were predominantly composed of disulfide-bonded α-la, β-lg, and κ-casein [46,47]. The IF (−5 °C) and IF (−10 °C) samples also displayed a lower intensity for the casein bands under native conditions when compared to fresh milk. However, these bands became visible in the gels after the application of the reducing reagent. The generation of aggregates following high pressure treatments was previously reported by Jiang et al. [48]. β-lg is the most sensitive whey protein to pressure and can undergo denaturation under certain pressure [48,49]. Previous studies have found that pressure treatments between 50 and 100 MPa led to a predenatured state of β-lg, which can be reversible [50]. Higher pressure treatments, such as 400 MPa, can induce intermolecular-disulfide bonds between β-lg and k-casein. HPP treatment with longer durations or higher pressures can also induce interactions between β-lg and casein micelles that lead to sedimentation [40]. Under reducing conditions, the casein proteins appeared as sharp bands, suggesting that the denatured proteins did not sediment out of the solution. Huppertz et al. [40] reported that the level of sedimentable denatured β-lg increases with pressures greater than 100 MPa. Additionally, under high pressure conditions ranging from 400 to 800 MPa for 30 min, up to 80% of β-lg has been observed to sediment. The results of this study indicated that protein sedimentation remained limited in both IF (−5 °C) and IF (−10 °C), even after 5 weeks of storage.

### 3.7. Lactoperoxidase Activity

Lactoperoxidase (LPO) in milk catalyzes oxidation reactions in the presence of hydrogen peroxide to produce antimicrobial compounds. Enzyme activity is dependent on many variables such as pH, environment, pressure, and temperature [51]. All treated samples showed nominal decreases in LPO activity when compared with fresh raw milk (Figure 6), with RF and HTST producing statistically significant decreases at 2 weeks, and all samples producing significant decreases at 5 weeks. HTST treatment immediately reduced LPO activity to 82% of the initial value. After two weeks, RF and HTST samples showed similar reductions in LPO activity to around 59% of the initial value. After 5 weeks, the HTST sample had an LPO activity that was 10% of the initial value. The IF (−5 °C) and IF (−10 °C) samples showed nominal but not statistically significant decreases in LPO activity after two weeks, to 72.5 and 80% of the initial value, respectively. After 5 weeks, both IF (−5 °C) and IF (−10 °C) samples showed no significant changes in LPO activity compared to their 2-week values, but passed the threshold of significance for difference from the initial sample. Duarte et al. [12] also observed a decrease in activity when applying similar pressures at room temperature. More work is required, perhaps for longer treatment periods, to determine the specific effects of IF treatment on enzyme activity.

### 3.8. SPME GC/MS Analysis

The volatile profile of the milk samples under the studied storage conditions was collected over a period of 5 weeks and the results are provided in Table 4. In total, 33 compounds consisting of five acids, five alcohols, seven aliphatic hydrocarbons, two aldehydes, two aromatics, two esters, nine ketones, and one nitrogenous compound were identified. Of these, 28 compounds were confirmed through their corresponding reference literature retention indices, while the remaining five compounds were tentatively identified using their mass spectra alone. Figure 7 provides a comparison of the aroma profile for all storage treatments. Here, the mean relative abundance of volatile compositional differences by chemical class is shown.

Although the milk’s profile is believed to be partially influenced by diet [52], the aroma composition found in the initial milk sample was consistent with findings in the literature [12,53]. The three most abundant compounds present in the initial milk sample were methoxyphenyl-oxime (36%), acetone (23%), and 2-butanone (13%). While there is little information regarding the flavor characteristics of methoxyphenyl-oxime, its presence in milk has been reported elsewhere [13,53]. Acetone and 2-butanone, both ketones, are common milk aromas which might originate from the cow’s metabolism. Ketone aromas contribute to floral or fruity aromas in milk. The remaining compounds are classified as free fatty acids (FFAs), branched hydrocarbons, alcohols, and aromatics. In the context of flavor, FFAs are of particular importance. FFAs can come from various sources, such as in the lipolysis of milk triglycerides, lipid oxidation reactions, or microbial growth. Thus, high concentrations of (volatile) FFAs suggests the degradation of milk quality and flavor.

After two weeks of storage, a significant increase (p < 0.05) in FFAs (~11×) was observed in the refrigerated samples (RF). In addition to the increase in all formerly identified FFAs, newly formed FFAs included butanoic acid and decanoic acid. Ethanol was also detected in the refrigerated raw milk samples only. The newly formed ester, ethyl acetate, contributes to the sourness of the milk and is an indicator of milk quality degradation. Significant increases in aliphatic hydrocarbons were also observed, however their impact on the milk’s flavor is considered secondary due to their high odor thresholds.

Same-day pasteurization of the initial milk sample did not result in substantial changes in nearly all chemical categories. However, small amounts of newly formed decanoic acid were detected. The formation of nonanal, which delivers sweet grass-like odors was also observed. Milk pasteurization followed by 2 weeks of refrigeration (HTST) led to a significant increase in aliphatic hydrocarbon content but a decline in overall ketone amounts. The net outcome of these changes likely signifies the onset of milk flavor degradation. However, if compared with RF results, HTST substantially improves preservation of milk flavor. By week 5, changes in HTST’s volatile profile were apparent as there was a ~50-fold increase in free fatty acid content suggesting milk spoilage.

IF treatments resulted in an overall better preservation of raw milk VOC profiles, even after 5 weeks, with no notable changes (p > 0.05) in FFAs and esters when compared to their initial values. Milk aroma profiles were also measured following isochoric freezing at −5 °C and −10 °C. Like the HTST findings, two weeks of IF storage resulted in relatively few significant changes in the aroma profile. The most significant change appears to be an increase in aliphatic hydrocarbons. Interestingly, the resulting aroma profiles between IF −5 °C and −10 °C were highly similar. Remarkably, 5 weeks of IF storage led to no substantive changes in the milk’s volatile profile from their 2-week measurements. Such findings suggest IF effectively preserves milk flavor for time periods much longer than conventional pasteurization techniques.

A principal components analysis was performed on the VOCs in order to identify possible relationships between storage conditions. Figure 8 plots the first two principal components (PC1 and PC2). The biplot shows that, apart from ketones, most chemical classes had high loadings in the first principal component. The sum of the first two PCs results in 71.5% of the variance being explained. As expected, isochoric samples are closely grouped to the initial milk sample.

## 4. Conclusions

This work describes the effects of isochoric freezing at −5 °C/77 MPa and 10 °C/96 MPa on the physicochemical properties, indigenous enzyme activity, protein content, volatile organic compounds profile, lipid degradation, and microbiological activity of raw bovine milk. Overall, prolonged storage under isochoric freezing conditions, when compared to refrigeration (RF), resulted in superior quality across measured parameters. Prolonged isochoric freezing was also able to better preserve milk for longer storage periods as compared to HTST treated milk. Unlike conventional refrigeration and HTST treatment, IF-treated milk at −5 °C/77 MPa and −10 °C/96 MPa not only inhibited microbial growth, but also significantly reduced the microbial count, with IF (−10 °C) producing counts below the detectable limit. This anti-microbial effect, driven by the combination of enhanced pressure and reduced temperature, enabled the shelf-life extension of raw milk for up to 5 weeks (the longest storage period studied).

At −10 °C/96 MPa, higher pressures resulted in faster and more effective microbial deactivation, but these conditions did impact the physicochemical properties when compared to unprocessed raw milk. In contrast, at −5 °C/77 MPa, the volatiles profile and lipid oxidation levels that were similar to fresh raw milk were retained at 5 weeks, and there were no physiochemical or microbiological indications that substantially longer storage would not be achievable.

Compared to available data on room-temperature hyperbaric storage at 75 MPa and 100 MPa, the combined high-pressure low-temperature conditions offered by isochoric freezing appear to reduce unfavorable changes in lipid oxidation and the volatiles profile in raw milk; though direct experimental comparison would be needed to definitively conclude as much. Furthermore, hyperbaric storage requires active mechanical induction of pressure, whereas isochoric freezing produces passive self-pressurization driven only by temperature. As such, this preservation technique may prove more practical and adaptable to existing milk production and storage processes; low-temperature control infrastructure is already omnipresent within the dairy processing and distribution industry, and thus the only additional equipment necessary for this treatment would be isochoric storage containers.

As a whole, this study indicates that isochoric freezing has the potential to significantly increase the shelf life of milk by reducing microbial activity, whilst maintaining its nutritional and physiochemical content. The application of isochoric freezing, with its potential to adjust milk’s shelf life without a significant deviation in quality, could offer a new means of reducing milk waste driven by temporal market fluctuations, and addressing future milk capacitance uncertainties driven by climate change. Future work might include isochoric treatment of non-raw milk products, an examination of the absolute limits of milk shelf life under isochoric conditions, and the study of the evolution of milk bacterial profile following prolonged isochoric storage.
